entries.1:1: Luke is writing a second book to a man named Theophilus, reminding him that his first book already covered everything Jesus did and taught. It shows the reader that this is a true, connected account of what happened next.
entries.1:2: This verse looks back to the day Jesus went up to heaven, after he had given instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles he had chosen. It reminds the reader that Jesus led and guided his chosen followers right up to the end.
entries.1:3: After his death, Jesus showed his followers many convincing proofs that he was really alive, appearing to them over forty days and teaching them about God's kingdom. It means the resurrection was a real, verified event, and the reader can trust it.
entries.1:4: While they were together, Jesus told his followers not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for what the Father had promised, which he had already told them about. It means some things must be waited for in obedience rather than chased after.
entries.1:5: John baptized people with water, but Jesus said his followers would soon be baptized with the Holy Spirit. It means God was about to give his people a new, deeper experience of his presence and power.
entries.1:6: The followers asked Jesus whether he was now going to restore the kingdom to Israel. It shows they were still thinking about political power, and the reader sees how easy it is to misunderstand what God is doing.
entries.1:7: Jesus told them it is not their business to know the times and dates the Father has set by his own authority. It means God keeps some timing to himself, and the reader should trust him rather than demand a schedule.
entries.1:8: You will receive power when the Spirit comes, and you will be witnesses. The power is for going, not for sitting.
entries.1:9: After saying this, Jesus was lifted up while they watched, and a cloud took him out of their sight. It means his departure was real and visible, and the reader is meant to see it as a true historical event.
entries.1:10: As they stared up at the sky, two men in white clothes suddenly stood beside them. It means God sent messengers to speak into their confusion, and the reader sees that heaven responds to human bewilderment.
entries.1:11: The two men asked why they were staring at the sky and said this same Jesus would come back in the same way they saw him go. It means Jesus' return is certain, and the reader can live with hope rather than just nostalgia.
entries.1:12: The followers returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, which is close to the city, about a Sabbath day's walk away. It simply grounds the story in a real place and distance, showing these events happened in actual geography.
entries.1:13: When they arrived, they went upstairs to the room where they were staying, and the verse lists the eleven apostles by name. It shows the reader that this was a specific, identifiable group of real people, not a vague crowd.
entries.1:14: They all joined together constantly in prayer, along with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. It means unity and prayer were central to the early church, and the reader is shown a model of depending on God together.
entries.1:15: In those days Peter stood up among the believers, about a hundred and twenty of them, and spoke. It shows Peter taking a lead role and gives the reader a sense of the size and shape of the early community.
entries.1:16: Peter said that Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit had spoken through David about Judas, who guided those who arrested Jesus. It means even betrayal was not outside God's foreknowledge, and the reader sees Scripture being taken seriously.
entries.1:17: Judas had been counted as one of them and shared in their ministry. It means he was genuinely part of the group, and the reader feels the weight of how close someone can be to Jesus and still fall away.
entries.1:18: This man bought a field with the money he got for his wicked act, and then fell headlong and his body burst open. It describes the grim end of Judas, and the reader sees that sin carries real and terrible consequences.
entries.1:19: Everyone living in Jerusalem heard about it, so the field was called Akeldama, which means Field of Blood. It means the story was public knowledge, and the reader sees that the consequences of sin became a lasting memorial.
entries.1:20: Peter quotes the Psalms, which say his home should be left empty and someone else should take his position. It means Scripture itself pointed to what needed to happen next, and the reader sees God's word guiding the community's decisions.
entries.1:21: So they needed someone who had been with them the whole time Jesus was among them. It means the replacement had to be an eyewitness, and the reader sees the importance of real, firsthand testimony.
entries.1:22: That person had to be a witness from John's baptism through to Jesus' ascension, and especially of his resurrection. It means the core message was the risen Jesus, and the reader sees what the church was built on.
entries.1:23: They put forward two men, Joseph called Barsabbas (also known as Justus) and Matthias. It shows the community making a careful, limited choice, and the reader sees a process rather than a free-for-all.
entries.1:24: They prayed and asked the Lord, who knows everyone's heart, to show which of the two he had chosen. It means they trusted God to decide, and the reader is shown prayer as the right response to uncertainty.
entries.1:25: They asked God to show who should take the place of ministry and apostleship that Judas left by his sin. It means the role mattered and needed filling properly, and the reader sees that failure doesn't cancel God's work.
entries.1:26: They cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias, who was then counted with the eleven apostles. It means they used a common method of the time to seek God's choice, and the reader sees the group restored to twelve.
entries.2:1: The followers of Jesus were gathered together in one place on the day of a Jewish festival called Pentecost. It means they were united and waiting, and it reminds the reader that God often works when his people come together.
entries.2:2: Suddenly a loud sound like a strong wind came from heaven and filled the whole house where they were sitting. It shows that something powerful from God was happening, and it tells the reader that God's presence can be felt and heard.
entries.2:3: They saw what looked like small flames of fire spreading out and resting on each person there. This was a visible sign that God was present with each one of them, not just the group as a whole.
entries.2:4: Everyone there was filled with the Holy Spirit and began speaking in other languages, just as the Spirit enabled them. It means God gave them the ability to speak in ways they normally could not, showing that he equips people for what he calls them to do.
entries.2:5: Many devout Jews from many different countries were living in Jerusalem at that time. This sets the scene: a wide mix of people was there to hear what God was about to do.
entries.2:6: When the crowd heard the noise, they gathered and were amazed to hear the disciples speaking in each person's own native language. It means God made his message understandable to each listener, and it shows he cares about reaching people where they are.
entries.2:7: The people were astonished and asked how this could be, since all these speakers were from Galilee. It means the speakers were ordinary people from a ordinary region, so the crowd knew this ability had to come from somewhere beyond them.
entries.2:8: Each person in the crowd was hearing the disciples speak in the language they had learned from birth. It means no one was left out because of a language barrier, and it shows God's message is for everyone.
entries.2:9: This lists people from Parthia, Media, Elam, Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, and Asia. It means the crowd came from many far-off places, showing how widely this moment reached.
entries.2:10: The list continues with people from Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, parts of Libya near Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, both Jews and converts to Judaism. It means the good news was reaching a very diverse group, including outsiders who had joined the faith.
entries.2:11: People from Crete and Arabia were also there, and they heard the disciples telling in their own languages about the great things God has done. It means the message was not just about ideas but about God's mighty acts, and it was being shared in a way everyone could understand.
entries.2:12: Everyone was amazed and confused, asking each other what this could possibly mean. It means people were genuinely puzzled and trying to make sense of what they saw, which is a normal first reaction to something from God.
entries.2:13: Some people, however, made fun of them and said they were drunk on new wine. It means not everyone responds seriously to God's work; some dismiss it, and the reader should not be surprised when that happens.
entries.2:14: Peter stood up with the eleven other apostles and spoke loudly to the crowd in Jerusalem, asking them to listen carefully. It means Peter took the lead and explained what was happening, showing that God's work deserves a clear explanation.
entries.2:15: Peter said these men were not drunk, since it was only nine in the morning. It means he answered the mockers with a simple fact, showing that the truth can be defended plainly.
entries.2:16: Peter said this was actually what the prophet Joel had spoken about long ago. It means what was happening was not random but part of God's long-planned purpose, which gives the reader confidence that God keeps his word.
entries.2:17: God says that in the last days he will pour out his Spirit on all kinds of people, and sons, daughters, young men, and old men will all receive dreams and visions. It means God's Spirit is not limited to a special few but is given broadly, including to ordinary people like the reader.
entries.2:18: God says he will pour out his Spirit even on servants, both men and women, and they will speak his message. It means status and gender do not shut anyone out from God's work, which is a strong statement of inclusion.
entries.2:19: God promises wonders in the sky and signs on the earth, including blood, fire, and smoke. It means God will act in ways that are visible and unmistakable, both in the heavens and on earth.
entries.2:20: The sun will go dark and the moon will turn red like blood before the great and glorious day of the Lord arrives. It means dramatic signs will come before God's final judgment, reminding the reader that history is moving toward a definite end.
entries.2:21: Everyone who calls on the Lord will be saved. It means salvation is available to anyone who turns to God, no matter who they are, which is a direct invitation to the reader.
entries.2:22: Peter told the people of Israel to listen: Jesus of Nazareth was a man approved by God, proven by the miracles and wonders God did through him among them, which they themselves saw. It means Jesus' identity was backed up by public evidence, not just claims.
entries.2:23: Jesus was handed over according to God's plan and foreknowledge, and the people put him to death by the hands of lawless men. It means both God's purpose and human guilt were involved in the cross, so the reader sees that evil was real even while God was working.
entries.2:24: But God raised Jesus back to life, freeing him from the pain of death, because death could not hold him. It means death was defeated, and the reader can have hope that death is not the final word.
entries.2:25: Peter quotes David, who said he kept the Lord always before him, and because the Lord was at his right hand, he would not be shaken. It means trusting God's constant presence gives stability, even in hard times.
entries.2:26: Because of this, David's heart was glad, his tongue rejoiced, and his body rested in hope. It means confidence in God produces real joy and peace, even about the future.
entries.2:27: David said God would not abandon his soul to the grave or let his Holy One decay. It means God does not desert his faithful one in death, which points forward to the resurrection.
entries.2:28: God made known the paths of life, and David said he would be full of joy in God's presence. It means God shows people how to live and gives lasting joy that comes from being near him.
entries.2:29: Peter pointed out plainly that David died, was buried, and his tomb was still there with them. It means David's words could not be fully about himself, since he clearly died and stayed dead.
entries.2:30: David was a prophet and knew God had sworn that one of his descendants would sit on his throne. It means David was speaking about a future king, which points to Jesus.
entries.2:31: Seeing ahead, David spoke of the Messiah's resurrection, that he would not be left in the grave and his body would not decay. It means the resurrection was predicted long before it happened, strengthening the reader's trust in the Bible's reliability.
entries.2:32: Peter declared that God raised this Jesus to life, and all of them were witnesses of it. It means the resurrection was not a rumor but something people saw, which gives the reader a solid basis for faith.
entries.2:33: Jesus was raised to God's right hand, received the promised Holy Spirit from the Father, and poured out what the crowd was now seeing and hearing. It means the events of that day were proof that Jesus is alive and active, not just a memory.
entries.2:34: Peter notes that David did not go up into heaven, yet David himself said the Lord told his Lord to sit at his right hand. It means David was pointing to someone greater than himself, namely the Messiah.
entries.2:35: God said he would put all of the Messiah's enemies under his feet. It means Jesus' enemies will ultimately be defeated, and the reader can trust that evil will not win in the end.
entries.2:36: Peter concluded that all Israel should be certain that God has made this same Jesus, whom they crucified, both Lord and Christ. It means Jesus' identity is not optional or unclear; he is the promised king, and the reader is called to recognize that.
entries.2:37: When the people heard this, they were cut to the heart and asked Peter and the apostles what they should do. It means the message hit home and produced real concern, showing that honest hearing of the truth leads to action.
entries.2:38: Repent, be baptised, and receive the gift of the Spirit. It is an invitation with a promise inside it.
entries.2:39: Peter said the promise is for them, for their children, and for everyone far off, as many as the Lord calls. It means God's offer is not limited to one group or generation, which includes the reader.
entries.2:40: Peter kept urging them with many more words, testifying and telling them to be saved from that crooked generation. It means he did not just give information but pressed them to respond and turn away from a corrupt way of life.
entries.2:41: Those who accepted his message were baptized, and about three thousand people joined them that day. It means many responded seriously, and the reader sees that a clear message can lead to real, large-scale change.
entries.2:42: The first believers made learning from the apostles, sharing meals, and praying a steady priority. It means we should build our lives around learning about Jesus and being with other believers, not just fitting faith in when it's convenient.
entries.2:43: People were deeply struck with awe, and the apostles performed many miracles that showed God's power. It reminds us that God was clearly at work in this community, and we should take his presence seriously.
entries.2:44: The believers stayed closely together and shared what they owned instead of treating it as private. It means real faith shows up in generosity and in treating other believers like family.
entries.2:45: They sold possessions and property and gave the money to anyone who needed it. It means we should be willing to use what we have to help others in need, not just hold onto everything for ourselves.
entries.2:46: They met together regularly at the Temple and shared meals in each other's homes with glad and sincere hearts. It means faith is meant to be lived out in everyday life with joy and honesty, alongside other believers.
entries.2:47: They praised God and were well thought of by the people around them, and the Lord kept adding to their number those who were being saved. It means when believers live this way, God is honored and draws others to himself, and the growth is his doing.
entries.3:1: Peter and John were heading to the Temple at the usual afternoon prayer time, showing they still kept their Jewish habits of worship. It reminds the reader that prayer was a normal, expected part of their day.
entries.3:2: A man who had never been able to walk was carried to the Temple gate every day to beg for money. His whole life depended on the generosity of people passing by.
entries.3:3: When the man saw Peter and John about to enter, he asked them for money. He was simply doing his daily job of begging.
entries.3:4: Peter looked straight at him, with John beside him, and told him to look at them. He wanted the man's full attention before anything happened.
entries.3:5: The man looked at them eagerly, expecting to receive some cash. He thought his need was money.
entries.3:6: Peter said he had no money to give, but he would give what he did have, and then commanded the man to stand up in the name of Jesus. The healing came from Jesus, not from Peter's wealth.
entries.3:7: Peter took him by the right hand and helped him up, and immediately his feet and ankles became strong. The healing was instant and complete.
entries.3:8: The man jumped up, stood, and went into the Temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God. His first response to being healed was joyful worship.
entries.3:9: Everyone in the Temple area saw the man walking and praising God. The healing was public and impossible to miss.
entries.3:10: People recognized him as the same beggar who had sat at the gate, and they were amazed and astonished. Something they thought could never change had changed.
entries.3:11: The healed man clung to Peter and John, and a crowd rushed toward them at Solomon's porch, stunned by what had happened. The miracle drew a crowd that would hear the message.
entries.3:12: Peter asked the crowd why they were so surprised and why they were staring at him and John as if they had healed the man by their own power. He wanted the credit to go to God, not to himself.
entries.3:13: Peter pointed to the God of Israel's ancestors, who had glorified his servant Jesus, the same Jesus the crowd had handed over to be killed even though Pilate wanted to release him. He named their guilt plainly but rooted it in God's action.
entries.3:14: They rejected the holy and righteous one and instead asked for a murderer to be set free. Peter contrasted their choice sharply with who Jesus actually was.
entries.3:15: They killed the one who is the source of life, but God raised him from the dead, and Peter and John were eyewitnesses of that. The resurrection is presented as a fact they personally saw.
entries.3:16: It was faith in the name of Jesus that made this man strong and completely well in front of everyone. The power came through trusting in Jesus, not through Peter.
entries.3:17: Peter acknowledged that the people and their leaders acted out of ignorance. He spoke to them as brothers rather than as enemies.
entries.3:18: God had foretold through all the prophets that the Messiah would suffer, and he fulfilled that plan through what happened. Even the rejection of Jesus was part of God's declared purpose.
entries.3:19: Peter called them to change their hearts and turn back to God so their sins could be wiped out and times of refreshment could come. Repentance is presented as the path to forgiveness and blessing.
entries.3:20: The goal of turning to God is that he may send the Messiah he had already appointed for them, namely Jesus. Their repentance was tied to God's future sending of Christ.
entries.3:21: Jesus must remain in heaven until the time when everything is restored, which God announced long ago through his holy prophets. There is a set future time for full restoration.
entries.3:22: Moses had said God would raise up a prophet like himself from among the people, and they must listen to everything he says. Peter identified Jesus as that promised prophet.
entries.3:23: Anyone who refuses to listen to that prophet will be cut off from the people. Rejecting the prophet God sends is a serious matter with real consequences.
entries.3:24: All the prophets from Samuel onward spoke about these very days. What was happening was not a new idea but the fulfillment of a long line of prophecy.
entries.3:25: The crowd were heirs of the prophets and of God's covenant with Abraham, in which God promised that all families on earth would be blessed through his offspring. They stood in a long line of promise.
entries.3:26: God sent his servant first to them, to bless them by turning each of them away from their sins. The blessing God offers is not just material but a changed life.
entries.4:1: Religious leaders and temple guards came up to Peter and John while they were still speaking to the crowd. It shows that speaking openly about Jesus can quickly bring opposition from people in power.
entries.4:2: These leaders were upset because the apostles taught that Jesus had risen from the dead, which they denied. The message of Jesus rising again still challenges people who reject it today.
entries.4:3: They arrested Peter and John and jailed them overnight because it was already late. Following Jesus can cost you your freedom, even when you have done nothing wrong.
entries.4:4: Many who heard the message believed, bringing the number of believers to about five thousand. Opposition cannot stop God's word from reaching and changing people.
entries.4:5: The next day the ruling council and legal experts gathered in Jerusalem. The most powerful people in the nation came together to deal with two ordinary men.
entries.4:6: The high priest and his family and associates were all present at this meeting. The highest religious authorities were united against the apostles.
entries.4:7: They brought Peter and John in and asked them by what power or authority they had healed the man. The leaders wanted to know the source of the miracle.
entries.4:8: Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke boldly to the rulers and elders. God gives ordinary people the right words when they are questioned about their faith.
entries.4:9: Peter pointed out that they were being questioned about a good deed done to a sick man. It is strange that doing good can land you in trouble.
entries.4:10: Peter declared that the man was healed by the name of Jesus, whom they had killed but God had raised from the dead. Jesus is alive and still has power to heal and save.
entries.4:11: Peter used the picture of a rejected stone that became the most important one in the building. Jesus, whom the leaders rejected, is the one God has made central to everything.
entries.4:12: Salvation is found in no one else, because no other name has been given by which people can be saved. Jesus is the only way to be saved, and that is true for everyone.
entries.4:13: The leaders were amazed that uneducated men spoke so boldly, and they realized these men had been with Jesus. Time spent with Jesus changes people and gives them courage.
entries.4:14: The healed man was standing right there with them, so the leaders had nothing to say against the miracle. Clear evidence of God's work silences opposition.
entries.4:15: The council sent Peter and John out of the room so they could discuss the matter privately. Even powerful leaders had to stop and figure out what to do.
entries.4:16: They admitted the miracle was obvious to everyone in Jerusalem and could not be denied. When God acts, even those who oppose him cannot ignore it.
entries.4:17: They decided to threaten the apostles so the message would not spread any further. People often try to silence the truth when they cannot disprove it.
entries.4:18: They ordered Peter and John to stop speaking or teaching in the name of Jesus. Following Jesus may mean facing pressure to keep quiet about him.
entries.4:19: Peter and John asked the leaders to judge whether it was right before God to obey them rather than God. When human orders conflict with God's command, we must obey God.
entries.4:20: They said they could not stop speaking about what they had seen and heard. When you have truly experienced Jesus, it is impossible to keep quiet about him.
entries.4:21: After more threats they released the apostles, because the people were praising God for the healing and they feared public reaction. God can use even crowd opinion to protect his people.
entries.4:22: The man who was healed was over forty years old, so this was no minor or temporary condition. The miracle was undeniable because the man had been lame his whole life.
entries.4:23: Once released, Peter and John went back to their friends and reported everything the leaders had said. Believers need each other to share burdens and pray together.
entries.4:24: The believers prayed together with one heart, addressing God as the Maker of heaven, earth, and sea. When facing threats, the right response is to turn to the God who made everything.
entries.4:25: They quoted David's words about nations raging and people plotting in vain. Opposition to God is nothing new and has always been futile.
entries.4:26: The psalm describes kings and rulers gathering together against the Lord and his chosen one. Human powers have always united against God's anointed, yet they cannot win.
entries.4:27: The believers saw this fulfilled when Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and Israel all joined against Jesus. Even the worst conspiracy against Jesus was part of God's plan.
entries.4:28: They acknowledged that everything done against Jesus had been determined beforehand by God's plan and purpose. God is sovereign even over the evil actions of people.
entries.4:29: They asked God to notice the threats and to give them boldness to keep preaching his word. Instead of praying for safety, they prayed for courage.
entries.4:30: They asked God to stretch out his hand to heal and to do signs and wonders through the name of Jesus. They wanted God's power to be seen so people would believe.
entries.4:31: After they prayed, the place shook and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke God's word boldly. God answers prayers for courage by filling his people with his Spirit.
entries.4:32: The believers were united in heart and mind, and no one claimed their possessions as their own but shared everything. True unity shows itself in generosity and care for one another.
entries.4:33: The apostles powerfully testified that Jesus had risen from the dead, and great grace was on them all. A church that shares generously is also a church that speaks boldly.
entries.4:34: No one among them was in need, because those who owned land or houses sold them. Generosity met real needs so that no one was left lacking.
entries.4:35: They brought the money to the apostles, who distributed it to each person according to need. The church organized its giving so that everyone was cared for fairly.
entries.4:36: Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, was nicknamed Barnabas, which means son of encouragement. A good nickname reflects a person's character, and Barnabas was known for encouraging others.
entries.4:37: He sold a field he owned and laid the money at the apostles' feet. Barnabas not only encouraged with words but also gave generously with his possessions.
entries.5:1: A man named Ananias and his wife Sapphira sold some property and received the money for it. This sets up the story of what they chose to do with that money.
entries.5:2: Ananias secretly kept part of the money for himself, with his wife's agreement, and brought the rest to the apostles as if it were the full amount. He was trying to look more generous than he really was.
entries.5:3: Peter asked Ananias why Satan had filled his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit by keeping back part of the money. His deception was not just against people but against God.
entries.5:4: Peter pointed out that the property and the money were always Ananias's to control, so no one forced him to give it. The sin was not about the amount but about lying to God.
entries.5:5: When Ananias heard this, he fell down dead, and everyone who heard about it was deeply afraid. The seriousness of lying to God became very real to the community.
entries.5:6: Some young men came, wrapped up his body, carried it out, and buried him. The story moves quickly from his sin to its consequences.
entries.5:7: About three hours later, his wife Sapphira came in, not knowing what had happened to her husband. She was about to face the same question.
entries.5:8: Peter asked her directly whether the money they gave was the full price of the land, and she said yes. She confirmed the same lie her husband had told.
entries.5:9: Peter asked why they had agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord, and told her the men who buried her husband were at the door ready to carry her out too. Her part in the deception was not hidden.
entries.5:10: She immediately fell down dead at Peter's feet, and the young men came in, found her dead, and buried her beside her husband. She shared in the same judgment as her husband.
entries.5:11: Great fear came over the whole church and everyone who heard about these events. The community learned that God takes sin and honesty seriously.
entries.5:12: The apostles performed many miraculous signs and wonders among the people, and the believers gathered together in Solomon's colonnade. God was clearly working through them.
entries.5:13: Outsiders were afraid to join them casually, but the people spoke highly of them. The believers were respected even though people kept their distance.
entries.5:14: More and more men and women believed in the Lord and were added to the church. Despite the fear, the message kept drawing people to faith.
entries.5:15: People brought the sick out into the streets on beds and mats so that Peter's shadow might fall on some of them as he passed by. They were desperate for healing and believed God could use even that.
entries.5:16: Crowds came from towns around Jerusalem bringing the sick and those troubled by evil spirits, and every one of them was healed. The power of God was reaching far beyond the city.
entries.5:17: The high priest and his associates, who were Sadducees, became filled with jealousy. They resented the apostles' influence and the attention they were getting.
entries.5:18: They arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail. The religious leaders tried to stop the movement by locking its leaders up.
entries.5:19: During the night, an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and led them out. God was not going to let his messengers be silenced.
entries.5:20: The angel told them to go stand in the temple courts and tell the people the full message about this new life. They were sent right back to the place they had been arrested for speaking.
entries.5:21: At dawn they went into the temple and began teaching, while the high priest and his council gathered and sent to the jail to have the apostles brought. Both sides were preparing for a confrontation.
entries.5:22: The officers sent to the jail found the apostles gone and returned to report it. The leaders' plan was already falling apart.
entries.5:23: They reported that the prison doors were securely locked and the guards were standing at the doors, but no one was inside. The escape was impossible to explain.
entries.5:24: The captain of the temple guard and the chief priests were puzzled and worried about where this could lead. They had no idea how to handle what was happening.
entries.5:25: Someone arrived and told them the men they had jailed were standing in the temple courts teaching the people. The apostles were doing exactly what they had been forbidden to do.
entries.5:26: The captain and his officers went and brought the apostles in without force, because they were afraid the people might stone them. They had to be careful how they handled this.
entries.5:27: They brought the apostles before the Sanhedrin, and the high priest questioned them. The official hearing had begun.
entries.5:28: The high priest reminded them that they had been strictly ordered not to teach in that name, yet they had filled Jerusalem with their teaching and were trying to make the council responsible for Jesus's death. He was angry that his orders had been ignored.
entries.5:29: Peter and the other apostles answered that they must obey God rather than human beings. When human authority conflicts with God's command, God comes first.
entries.5:30: They declared that the God of their ancestors had raised Jesus to life, the same Jesus the council had killed by hanging him on a cross. They were boldly naming the leaders' own guilt.
entries.5:31: God exalted Jesus to his right hand as Leader and Savior to give Israel repentance and forgiveness of sins. The very one they rejected is the one God made both Lord and Savior.
entries.5:32: The apostles said they were witnesses of these things, along with the Holy Spirit, whom God gives to those who obey him. Their testimony was backed by God himself.
entries.5:33: When the council heard this, they were furious and wanted to put the apostles to death. The truth made them angry rather than repentant.
entries.5:34: A Pharisee named Gamaliel, a respected teacher of the law, stood up and asked for the apostles to be sent outside for a while. He wanted to calm the situation and give his advice.
entries.5:35: Gamaliel warned the council to be careful about what they did to these men. He urged caution rather than a rushed decision.
entries.5:36: He reminded them of Theudas, who claimed to be somebody important and gathered about four hundred followers, but was killed and his movement fell apart. He was giving an example of failed movements.
entries.5:37: He also mentioned Judas of Galilee, who led people during the census, but he too was killed and his followers scattered. Gamaliel was building a case from history.
entries.5:38: Gamaliel advised the council to leave the apostles alone, saying that if their plan or work was merely human, it would fail on its own. He believed time would reveal the truth.
entries.5:39: But if it is from God, he warned, they would not be able to stop it and might even find themselves fighting against God. His advice was to let God settle the matter.
entries.5:40: The council agreed with Gamaliel, called the apostles in, had them flogged, ordered them not to speak in Jesus's name, and released them. The apostles were punished but not killed.
entries.5:41: The apostles left the council rejoicing because they had been counted worthy to be dishonored for Jesus' name. It means that being mistreated for your faith can be a reason for joy, not shame, since you are sharing in what happened to Jesus.
entries.5:42: The apostles kept teaching every day, both publicly in the temple and from house to house, telling people that Jesus is the Messiah. It means they did not let opposition stop them, and it encourages the reader to keep sharing and living out the message of Jesus consistently.
entries.6:1: As the church grew, Greek-speaking Jewish believers complained that their widows were being overlooked in the daily food distribution. It shows that even growing churches can have unfairness that needs to be fixed.
entries.6:2: The apostles told the gathered believers it wasn't right for them to stop teaching God's word in order to manage food distribution. It means leaders should stay focused on their main calling rather than trying to do everything.
entries.6:3: The apostles asked the believers to choose seven men with a good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to handle this task. It means practical service in the church should be given to trustworthy, spiritually mature people.
entries.6:4: The apostles said they would devote themselves to prayer and teaching the word. It reminds readers that prayer and teaching deserve serious, ongoing attention.
entries.6:5: The whole group was pleased with this plan and chose Stephen, Philip, and five others, including Nicolas. It shows the church working together to solve a problem in an orderly way.
entries.6:6: They brought the seven men to the apostles, who prayed and laid hands on them. It means the church set these men apart for service with prayer and public recognition.
entries.6:7: God's word kept spreading, the number of disciples in Jerusalem grew greatly, and many priests became obedient to the faith. It shows that handling problems well can help the church grow.
entries.6:8: Stephen, full of grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. It means God was working powerfully through an ordinary servant chosen to handle food distribution.
entries.6:9: Some men from several synagogues, including freedmen, Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and others from Cilicia and Asia, began arguing with Stephen. It shows that doing God's work can bring opposition from unexpected places.
entries.6:10: They could not match Stephen's wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke. It means God can give ordinary believers the right words to answer those who oppose them.
entries.6:11: They secretly persuaded men to claim Stephen had spoken blasphemy against Moses and God. It shows how opponents may resort to lies when they cannot win an argument.
entries.6:12: They stirred up the people, elders, and scribes, seized Stephen, and brought him before the Sanhedrin. It means false accusations can lead to serious trouble for innocent people.
entries.6:13: They brought false witnesses who claimed Stephen constantly spoke against the holy place and the law. It shows that even religious courts can be misled by dishonest testimony.
entries.6:14: The witnesses said Stephen claimed Jesus of Nazareth would destroy the temple and change the customs Moses handed down. It means his accusers twisted his teaching about Jesus into a charge of attacking their religion.
entries.6:15: Everyone in the Sanhedrin looked at Stephen and saw his face was like an angel's face. It means God gave him a calm, radiant presence even while he was being falsely accused.
entries.7:1: The high priest is officially asking Stephen whether the charges against him are true. This is the moment when Stephen must answer for his faith before the most powerful religious court.
entries.7:2: Stephen begins his defense by respectfully addressing the crowd and recalling how God appeared to Abraham while he was still living far from the promised land. It reminds the reader that God starts his work with ordinary people in unlikely places.
entries.7:3: God told Abraham to leave his homeland and relatives and go to a land God himself would show him. Following God often means stepping out without knowing all the details in advance.
entries.7:4: Abraham obeyed, leaving the Chaldean region and settling in Haran until his father died, and then God led him into the land where Stephen's hearers now lived. This shows God's promises unfold step by step over time.
entries.7:5: God promised Abraham the whole land as an inheritance for his descendants, even though Abraham owned no ground at all and had no child yet. God's promises can be true long before we see any evidence of them.
entries.7:6: God warned Abraham that his descendants would live as strangers in a foreign country and be mistreated as slaves for four hundred years. God tells his people ahead of time that hard seasons will come, but they are not the end of the story.
entries.7:7: God promised to judge the nation that enslaved them, and afterward his people would come out and worship him in that place. God does not ignore injustice, and he brings his people through hardship to worship.
entries.7:8: God made a covenant with Abraham, and circumcision was its sign; Abraham then passed it on to Isaac, and Isaac to Jacob, whose twelve sons became the heads of Israel's tribes. God keeps his promises from one generation to the next.
entries.7:9: Joseph's brothers were jealous of him and sold him into slavery in Egypt, yet God stayed with him through it all. Even when people treat us badly, God does not abandon us.
entries.7:10: God rescued Joseph from every trouble and gave him such wisdom that Pharaoh put him in charge of Egypt and his whole household. God can lift someone from the lowest place to a position of great responsibility.
entries.7:11: Famine struck all of Egypt and Canaan, and there was great suffering, so the ancestors of Israel could not find food. Hard times can hit whole regions, and even God's people are not spared from them.
entries.7:12: When Jacob heard there was grain in Egypt, he sent his sons there for the first time. God often provides help through unexpected places and people.
entries.7:13: On their second visit Joseph revealed himself to his brothers, and Pharaoh learned who Joseph's family was. What was hidden eventually comes to light, and reconciliation becomes possible.
entries.7:14: Joseph then sent for his father Jacob and the whole family, seventy-five people in all. God used Joseph's position to bring a divided family back together and provide for them.
entries.7:15: Jacob went down to Egypt and died there, and so did his sons. Even the promised family ended their lives in a foreign land, showing that God's plan often unfolds far from where we expect.
entries.7:16: Their bodies were later carried to Shechem and buried in the plot Abraham had bought from the sons of Hamor. This ties the story back to the land God had promised, even in death.
entries.7:17: As the time approached for God to fulfill his promise to Abraham, the people of Israel grew numerous in Egypt. God's timing is not idle; he works quietly until the moment is right.
entries.7:18: Then a new king came to power in Egypt who knew nothing about Joseph. Good times can end suddenly when leadership changes and past kindnesses are forgotten.
entries.7:19: This king schemed against Israel and treated them cruelly, forcing them to abandon their newborn children so they would die. Evil leaders can target the most vulnerable, but God sees it.
entries.7:20: At that very time Moses was born, and he was a fine child, so his family hid him for three months. God often brings a deliverer into the world right in the middle of oppression.
entries.7:21: When Moses could no longer be hidden, Pharaoh's daughter took him in and raised him as her own son. God can protect his chosen servant even inside the house of the enemy.
entries.7:22: Moses was educated in all the wisdom of Egypt and became powerful in speech and action. God can use skills learned in unlikely places for his purposes.
entries.7:23: When Moses was about forty, he decided to visit his own people, the Israelites. God plants a sense of identity and calling in a person's heart that eventually draws them to their true family.
entries.7:24: Seeing an Israelite being mistreated, Moses defended him and killed the Egyptian. A desire for justice is good, but acting on our own timing and methods can lead to trouble.
entries.7:25: Moses assumed his people would understand that God was using him to rescue them, but they did not. Sometimes we see a calling clearly while others around us do not.
entries.7:26: The next day Moses found two Israelites fighting and tried to make peace, reminding them they were brothers. Peacemaking is right, but it is not always welcomed.
entries.7:27: The man who was in the wrong pushed Moses away and asked who had made him ruler and judge over them. People often resist help and resent anyone who tries to correct them.
entries.7:28: He then threatened Moses, asking if he planned to kill him the way he had killed the Egyptian. Our past actions can be thrown back at us, and fear of exposure can drive us away.
entries.7:29: Frightened by those words, Moses fled to Midian, where he lived as a foreigner and had two sons. A setback sent him into years of obscurity, but God was not finished with him.
entries.7:30: After forty years, an angel appeared to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in a flame burning within a thorn bush. God often calls people after long seasons of waiting and hiddenness.
entries.7:31: Moses was amazed at the sight and went closer to look, and then the voice of the Lord spoke to him. Curiosity can lead us right into an encounter with God.
entries.7:32: God identified himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and Moses trembled and was afraid to look. The God who called the ancestors is the same God speaking now, and he deserves our reverence.
entries.7:33: The Lord told Moses to take off his sandals because the ground where he stood was holy. Ordinary places become sacred when God shows up, and we should treat them with respect.
entries.7:34: God said he had seen the suffering of his people, heard their cries, and come down to set them free, and he was sending Moses to Egypt. God notices the pain of his people and acts, often through a person he calls.
entries.7:35: The same Moses the Israelites rejected as a ruler and judge was the one God sent as ruler and deliverer through the angel in the burning bush. God often chooses the person others have dismissed.
entries.7:36: Moses led the people out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years. God's deliverance is backed by real, visible acts throughout a long journey.
entries.7:37: This same Moses told the Israelites that God would raise up a prophet from among their brothers like him. Moses pointed forward to someone greater who would come from their own people.
entries.7:38: Moses was with the assembly in the wilderness, along with the angel who spoke to him at Sinai and with the ancestors, and he received living words from God to pass on. God's words are living and meant to be handed down, not kept to ourselves.
entries.7:39: But the ancestors refused to obey Moses and pushed him aside, turning back to Egypt in their hearts. It is possible to be led by God and still long for the old life.
entries.7:40: They told Aaron to make them gods to lead them, saying they had no idea what had happened to Moses who brought them out of Egypt. People quickly forget God's deliverance and look for something visible to follow instead.
entries.7:41: The people made a gold statue of a calf and worshiped it, celebrating something they had made themselves. It warns us that we can easily replace God with things we create and control.
entries.7:42: God let the people go their own way and worship the stars instead of him, and through the prophets he asked whether their sacrifices were really meant for him. It shows that ignoring God can lead to being handed over to our own wrong choices.
entries.7:43: They carried idols of false gods like Moloch and Rephan, so God said he would send them far away in exile. It reminds us that worshiping other things instead of God has real consequences.
entries.7:44: In the desert the Israelites had a tent of worship made exactly as God instructed Moses. It shows that God takes seriously how he wants to be worshiped, not how we invent.
entries.7:45: The people brought that tent with them into the land as God drove out the nations, and it lasted until David's time. It shows God's faithful presence with his people through generations.
entries.7:46: David pleased God and wanted to build a special tent for him. It shows that loving God includes wanting to honor him, even if we don't get to finish the work.
entries.7:47: Solomon actually built the temple for God. It marks the moment Israel had a permanent house of worship instead of a tent.
entries.7:48: Even so, the Most High God does not live in buildings people make. It reminds us that no church building can contain God or be his true home.
entries.7:49: God says heaven is his throne and earth his footstool, so no building we make could ever be a proper house for him. It keeps us humble about our places of worship.
entries.7:50: God points out that his own hand made everything. It means the Creator needs nothing from us, and we owe him everything.
entries.7:51: Stephen tells his hearers they are stubborn and resistant to the Holy Spirit, just like their ancestors. It warns us against hardening our hearts when God speaks.
entries.7:52: Their ancestors persecuted and killed the prophets who announced the coming of the Righteous One, and now they had betrayed and murdered him. It shows how people can reject God's messengers and even God's Son.
entries.7:53: They received God's law through angels but did not obey it. It reminds us that hearing God's commands means nothing if we don't keep them.
entries.7:54: When they heard this, they were furious and ground their teeth at Stephen. It shows how truth can make people angry when they don't want to change.
entries.7:55: Full of the Holy Spirit, Stephen looked into heaven and saw God's glory with Jesus standing at his right hand. It shows that God's presence and honor for Jesus are real even when people reject him.
entries.7:56: Stephen announced that he could see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand. It shows Jesus is honored in heaven even as his follower is being attacked on earth.
entries.7:57: They shouted, covered their ears, and rushed at him together. It shows how people can shut out the truth and turn to violence rather than listen.
entries.7:58: They dragged him out of the city and stoned him, while the witnesses left their coats with a young man named Saul. It introduces Saul, who would later become Paul, showing how God can transform even a persecutor.
entries.7:59: As he was being stoned, Stephen prayed to Jesus to receive his spirit. It shows his trust in Jesus right to the end and that Jesus is someone we can pray to.
entries.7:60: Stephen knelt and asked God not to hold this sin against them, then he died. It shows a remarkable forgiveness that mirrors Jesus and challenges us to forgive even our enemies.
entries.8:1: A young man named Saul stood by and approved of Stephen being killed. That same day a fierce persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, so most believers scattered throughout Judea and Samaria, though the apostles stayed.
entries.8:2: Devout men buried Stephen's body and mourned deeply over him. It shows that even in terrible loss, honoring the dead and grieving openly is right.
entries.8:3: Saul violently attacked the church, going from house to house and dragging off men and women to prison. This shows how far someone can go against God before God turns him around.
entries.8:4: The believers who had fled went everywhere telling people the message about Jesus. God used the persecution to spread the good news far beyond Jerusalem.
entries.8:5: Philip went to a city in Samaria and preached to the people there about Christ. He took the message to a group that Jews usually avoided.
entries.8:6: The crowds paid close attention to what Philip said because they saw the miracles he performed. Miracles got their attention, but the message was what mattered.
entries.8:7: Evil spirits came out of many people with loud cries, and many who were sick or disabled were healed. The power of God was visibly at work among them.
entries.8:8: The whole town was filled with great joy. When God's power touches a place, it brings real happiness.
entries.8:9: A man named Simon had been practicing magic in Samaria and amazing the people, claiming he himself was someone great. He had built a following around his own reputation.
entries.8:10: Everyone, from the least to the greatest, listened to him and said he was the great power of God. People were quick to treat a impressive man as if he were divine.
entries.8:11: They had followed him for a long time because his magic had held them under his spell. Long habit made it hard for them to see past him.
entries.8:12: But when they believed Philip's good news about God's kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, many men and women were baptized. Faith in the message, not magic, is what saves.
entries.8:13: Simon himself believed and was baptized, and he followed Philip around, amazed at the signs and great miracles he saw. Even someone with a mixed heart can be drawn in by the power of God.
entries.8:14: When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted God's word, they sent Peter and John to them. The church checked on and supported new believers in a place they once despised.
entries.8:15: When Peter and John arrived, they prayed that these new believers would receive the Holy Spirit. New faith needs the Spirit's help, not just the right words.
entries.8:16: The Holy Spirit had not yet come on any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Baptism alone is not the whole story.
entries.8:17: Then the apostles placed their hands on them, and the Holy Spirit came on them. God confirmed that these Samaritan believers were fully part of his people.
entries.8:18: When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the apostles' hands, he offered them money. He wanted the power of God as something he could buy and control.
entries.8:19: He asked them to give him this power so that anyone he laid hands on would receive the Holy Spirit. He was treating a gift of God like a tool for his own use.
entries.8:20: Peter told him that his money should perish with him, because he thought God's free gift could be bought with cash. God's gifts are given, not sold.
entries.8:21: Peter said Simon had no part in this work because his heart was not right before God. Being involved in God's work requires a heart that is honest before him.
entries.8:22: Peter told him to change his heart and pray to God for forgiveness for his evil thoughts. There is still hope when someone turns to God honestly.
entries.8:23: Peter said he could see Simon was trapped in bitter envy and bound by sin. Sin can hold a person like chains, and it needs to be broken.
entries.8:24: Simon asked Peter to pray to the Lord for him so that none of these things would happen to him. He was frightened by the warning and wanted help.
entries.8:25: After Peter and John had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the good news in many Samaritan villages along the way. They did not waste the trip.
entries.8:26: An angel of the Lord told Philip to get up and go south to the road from Jerusalem down to Gaza, through the desert. God sometimes sends his people to unlikely, empty places.
entries.8:27: Philip went, and there was an Ethiopian official, a high servant of Candace the queen of the Ethiopians, in charge of all her treasure, who had come to Jerusalem to worship. God had prepared a seeker far from home.
entries.8:28: He was riding home in his carriage, reading the book of the prophet Isaiah. Even a powerful official was searching the Scriptures for answers.
entries.8:29: The Spirit told Philip to go near and get into the carriage. God guides his people to specific people at specific moments.
entries.8:30: Philip ran up and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and asked if he understood what he was reading. A simple question opened the door to a conversation about faith.
entries.8:31: The man said, How can I, unless someone guides me? And he invited Philip to sit beside him. It is honest to admit we need help understanding the Bible.
entries.8:32: The passage he was reading said that he was led like a sheep to be killed, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, he made no sound. It describes someone suffering quietly and unjustly.
entries.8:33: It said he was humbled and denied justice, and asked who could describe his generation, for his life was cut off from the earth. It pictures a life ended unfairly.
entries.8:34: The Ethiopian asked Philip whether the prophet was talking about himself or about someone else. He wanted to know who this suffering figure was.
entries.8:35: Starting from that very passage, Philip told him the good news about Jesus. The whole Bible points to Jesus, even the parts that seem unclear.
entries.8:36: As they traveled, they came to some water, and the Ethiopian asked why he could not be baptized. He wanted to respond to what he had just believed.
entries.8:37: This verse says that before someone could be baptized, they had to believe in Jesus with all their heart, and the man answered that he did. It means faith is the key requirement, so the reader is reminded that baptism follows genuine personal trust in Jesus, not just going through a ritual.
entries.8:38: He ordered the carriage to stop, and both of them went down into the water, and Philip baptized him. The man believed and was baptized right away.
entries.8:39: When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the Ethiopian saw him no more, but went on his way full of joy. He left with joy even though his teacher was gone.
entries.8:40: Philip ended up in Azotus and traveled through all the towns, preaching the good news until he reached Caesarea. He kept sharing the message wherever he went.
entries.9:1: Saul was still determined to hunt down and kill followers of Jesus, so he went to the high priest for support. This shows how fiercely someone can oppose God before God changes them.
entries.9:2: He asked for official letters so he could arrest Christians in Damascus and drag them back to Jerusalem. He wanted permission to treat believers as criminals wherever he found them.
entries.9:3: On the road to Damascus, a bright light from heaven suddenly flashed around him. God interrupted his plans in a way he could not ignore.
entries.9:4: Saul fell to the ground and heard a voice calling his name and asking why he was persecuting him. Jesus takes personally the way his followers are treated.
entries.9:5: Saul asked who was speaking, and the answer was Jesus himself, the one Saul was fighting against. Attacking Christians is attacking Jesus.
entries.9:6: Jesus told him to get up and go into the city, where he would learn what to do next. Sometimes God gives us only the next step, not the whole plan.
entries.9:7: The men traveling with Saul heard the voice but saw no one, and they were speechless. The encounter was real, even though only Saul understood what was said.
entries.9:8: Saul got up but could not see, so his companions led him by the hand into Damascus. The proud persecutor was now helpless and dependent on others.
entries.9:9: For three days he was blind and refused food or drink. He had time to sit with what had happened and to be humbled.
entries.9:10: In Damascus a disciple named Ananias heard the Lord call him in a vision, and he answered that he was ready. God still speaks to ordinary believers and expects a response.
entries.9:11: The Lord told Ananias to go to a specific house on Straight Street and look for Saul of Tarsus, who was praying. God knows exactly where people are and what they are doing.
entries.9:12: Saul had seen in a vision a man named Ananias coming to lay hands on him so he could see again. God was already preparing both men for the meeting.
entries.9:13: Ananias objected, saying he had heard how much harm Saul had done to believers in Jerusalem. It is natural to be afraid of someone with a violent past.
entries.9:14: He added that Saul had official authority to arrest everyone who called on the Lord's name. Ananias had good reason to hesitate.
entries.9:15: The Lord told him to go anyway, because Saul was his chosen instrument to carry his name to non-Jews, kings, and Israel. God can use even the worst enemy for his purposes.
entries.9:16: Jesus said he would show Saul how much suffering he would face for his name. Following Jesus does not mean an easy life, and God is honest about that.
entries.9:17: Ananias went, laid his hands on Saul, and called him brother, explaining that Jesus had sent him so Saul could see and be filled with the Holy Spirit. The man who came to arrest believers was welcomed as family.
entries.9:18: Something like scales fell from his eyes, he could see again, and he was baptized. His physical healing and his new start with God happened together.
entries.9:19: After eating, his strength returned, and he stayed with the disciples in Damascus for some days. He was now living among the very people he had planned to arrest.
entries.9:20: Right away he began preaching in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God. The man who opposed Jesus now spoke boldly for him.
entries.9:21: Everyone who heard him was amazed, asking if this was the same man who had attacked believers in Jerusalem and come to arrest them. A changed life makes people stop and wonder.
entries.9:22: Saul grew stronger in his arguments and proved to the Jews in Damascus that Jesus is the Messiah, leaving them unable to answer. God can give great confidence and clarity to someone he has turned around.
entries.9:23: After some days, the Jews in Damascus plotted together to kill him. Speaking the truth can make enemies, even when you are doing what is right.
entries.9:24: Saul learned of the plot, and they watched the city gates day and night to catch and kill him. Danger was closing in from every side.
entries.9:25: His followers took him at night and lowered him over the city wall in a basket. Sometimes escape and help from friends is the wise way out.
entries.9:26: When Saul reached Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid and did not believe he was really a disciple. People who knew his past found it hard to trust his change.
entries.9:27: Barnabas took Saul to the apostles and told them how he had seen the Lord on the road and had preached boldly in Damascus. One person willing to vouch for someone can open the door for them.
entries.9:28: After that, Saul stayed with them and moved freely around Jerusalem. He was now accepted as part of the community he had once persecuted.
entries.9:29: He preached boldly in the Lord's name and debated with Greek-speaking Jews, who then tried to kill him. Bold faith can stir up strong opposition.
entries.9:30: When the believers learned of the threat, they took him to Caesarea and sent him back to his hometown of Tarsus. Sometimes the wise move is to step away from danger for a while.
entries.9:31: The church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria then had peace, grew stronger, lived in reverence for the Lord, and was encouraged by the Holy Spirit, and it grew. Calm times and trust in God can help a church flourish.
entries.9:32: As Peter traveled through the region, he came to visit the believers living in Lydda. Leaders who go to ordinary believers and spend time with them strengthen the church.
entries.9:33: There he found a man named Aeneas who had been paralyzed and bedridden for eight years. Long-term suffering was not hidden from God.
entries.9:34: Peter told him that Jesus Christ heals him, and told him to get up and make his bed, and he did so at once. The healing came from Jesus, not from Peter's own power.
entries.9:35: Everyone living in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord. A visible change in one person's life can lead many others to God.
entries.9:36: In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, also called Dorcas, who was always doing good works and helping people in need. Her faith showed itself in practical kindness.
entries.9:37: She became sick and died, and after her body was washed, they laid her in an upstairs room. Even faithful, generous people face illness and death.
entries.9:38: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples there heard Peter was nearby and sent two men to ask him to come at once. They turned to a trusted leader in their grief.
entries.9:39: Peter went with them, and when he arrived, the widows stood around him crying and showing the clothes Dorcas had made for them. Her kindness was remembered in concrete ways by the people she had helped.
entries.9:40: Peter sent everyone out, knelt and prayed, then told Tabitha to get up, and she opened her eyes and sat up. He depended on God in prayer before anything happened.
entries.9:41: Peter took the dead woman by the hand and helped her up, and she came back to life. Then he called the believers and the widows in to see her alive, so they could share in the joy and know it really happened.
entries.9:42: Word of this miracle spread all over the town of Joppa, and many people came to believe in Jesus because of it. When God does something good, it can draw others toward him.
entries.9:43: Peter stayed in Joppa for a while, living with a man named Simon who worked with leather. This shows Peter was an ordinary guest in an ordinary home, not set apart in some special place.
entries.10:1: A Roman army officer named Cornelius lived in Caesarea. He was an important man, but the story shows that God notices ordinary people too, whatever their rank or background.
entries.10:2: Cornelius took God seriously, prayed regularly, and gave generously to the poor, and his whole household followed his example. His life shows that sincere faith shows up in how we treat God and other people.
entries.10:3: One afternoon Cornelius clearly saw an angel in a vision, and the angel called him by name. This reminds us that God can reach anyone directly and knows each person personally.
entries.10:4: Cornelius was afraid and asked what the angel wanted; the angel told him that his prayers and generosity had been noticed by God. Nothing good you do for God goes unseen, even when you feel overlooked.
entries.10:5: The angel told Cornelius to send for a man named Peter in Joppa. God was arranging a meeting that would change Cornelius's life.
entries.10:6: Peter was staying with a leather-worker named Simon, whose house was by the sea. The angel gave exact directions so Cornelius's men could find him.
entries.10:7: As soon as the angel left, Cornelius sent two servants and a trusted soldier to fetch Peter. He acted right away on what God told him.
entries.10:8: Cornelius explained everything to them and sent them off to Joppa. He didn't keep God's message to himself; he got others involved.
entries.10:9: The next day, as the men neared the town, Peter went up on the roof to pray around noon. Even a busy leader made time to pray.
entries.10:10: Peter was hungry while food was being prepared, and he fell into a deep sleep or trance. God used an ordinary moment of hunger and rest to speak to him.
entries.10:11: In the vision Peter saw heaven open and something like a large sheet being lowered to the ground. God was about to show him something new.
entries.10:12: The sheet was full of all kinds of animals and birds. This was a strange and troubling sight for a Jewish man like Peter.
entries.10:13: A voice told Peter to get up and eat the animals. God was asking him to do something he had always believed was wrong.
entries.10:14: Peter refused, saying he had never eaten anything unclean in his whole life. It's honest to tell God when something feels wrong to us.
entries.10:15: The voice answered that Peter must not call unclean what God has made clean. God has the right to change our long-held assumptions.
entries.10:16: This happened three times, then the sheet was taken back to heaven. The repetition shows this was important and not a random dream.
entries.10:17: Peter was still puzzled about the vision when Cornelius's men arrived at the gate looking for him. God's timing often lines up in ways we only see afterward.
entries.10:18: The men called out to ask whether Simon Peter was staying there. They were simply following the directions they'd been given.
entries.10:19: While Peter was still thinking it over, the Spirit told him three men were looking for him. God doesn't leave us guessing when we need guidance.
entries.10:20: The Spirit told Peter to go with them without hesitation because God had sent them. When God clearly directs, we can move forward without fear.
entries.10:21: Peter went down and identified himself, then asked why they had come. He was open to finding out what God was doing.
entries.10:22: They explained that Cornelius, a respected and God-fearing officer, had been told by an angel to send for Peter and listen to him. God was working on both ends of this meeting.
entries.10:23: Peter invited them in for the night, and the next day he went with them, taking some fellow believers along. He didn't go alone into something unfamiliar.
entries.10:24: They arrived in Caesarea, where Cornelius had gathered his relatives and close friends to hear Peter. He wanted others to share in what God was doing.
entries.10:25: When Peter arrived, Cornelius fell at his feet and worshipped him. He was overwhelmed with respect for God's messenger.
entries.10:26: Peter lifted him up and said he was just a man like Cornelius. No human leader should be treated as if they were God.
entries.10:27: Peter went inside and saw a large crowd gathered. This was going to be a significant moment for many people, not just Cornelius.
entries.10:28: Peter explained that Jewish custom kept him from associating with Gentiles, but God had shown him not to call any person common or unclean. God had changed his heart about people, not just about food.
entries.10:29: Peter said he came without objection when sent for, and asked why they had called him. He was ready to hear their side of the story.
entries.10:30: Cornelius explained that four days earlier, while praying at the same afternoon hour, he had seen a man in shining clothes. God had been preparing him for this very moment.
entries.10:31: The angel told him his prayer had been heard and his generosity remembered by God. God pays attention to both our words and our actions.
entries.10:32: The angel told him to send to Joppa for Simon Peter, who was staying with Simon the leather-worker by the sea. God gave clear, practical instructions.
entries.10:33: Cornelius said he sent for Peter immediately and was glad he came, and now everyone was gathered before God to hear what the Lord had told him. They came expecting to hear from God.
entries.10:34: Peter said he now clearly understood that God does not play favorites. God treats people fairly regardless of their background.
entries.10:35: In every nation, the person who respects God and does what is right is pleasing to him. What matters to God is a sincere heart and right actions, not where you're from.
entries.10:36: God sent a message to Israel: good news of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all. This peace is available to everyone, not just one group.
entries.10:37: Peter reminded them they already knew about this message that spread through Judea, starting in Galilee after John's baptism. The story of Jesus was already widely known.
entries.10:38: Peter described how God empowered Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit, and how Jesus went around doing good and healing people oppressed by evil spirits, because God was with him. Jesus's life was marked by kindness and power from God.
entries.10:39: Peter and the others were eyewitnesses to everything Jesus did in Judea and Jerusalem, and they saw him put to death on a cross. The witnesses were real people who saw it happen.
entries.10:40: But on the third day God raised Jesus back to life and let him be seen. Death was not the end of the story.
entries.10:41: Jesus didn't show himself alive after his death to the general public, but only to chosen witnesses. Those witnesses ate and drank with him, which proves he was really alive and not a ghost.
entries.10:42: Jesus told these witnesses to tell everyone the good news and to testify openly. Their message was that God has appointed Jesus to judge everyone, both the living and the dead.
entries.10:43: All the prophets spoke about Jesus, saying that anyone who believes in him will have their sins forgiven. Forgiveness comes through faith in him, not through anything else.
entries.10:44: Right in the middle of Peter's speech, the Holy Spirit came on everyone listening to the message. God acted while the word was being preached, showing he was at work.
entries.10:45: The Jewish believers who came with Peter were amazed that the Holy Spirit was given to non-Jews too. This showed them God's gift wasn't limited to their own people.
entries.10:46: The new believers were speaking in other languages and praising God, which was clear evidence the Spirit was on them. Seeing this, Peter spoke up.
entries.10:47: Peter asked whether anyone could object to baptizing people who had received the Holy Spirit just as the Jewish believers had. Since God had clearly accepted them, no one could refuse them baptism.
entries.10:48: Peter ordered that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Afterward they asked him to stay with them for a while, showing their new faith and friendship.
entries.11:1: The apostles and believers in Judea heard that non-Jewish people had also received God's message. This shows God's message is for everyone, not just one group.
entries.11:2: When Peter returned to Jerusalem, some believers who insisted on circumcision confronted him about what he had done. Even faithful people sometimes argue over who belongs to God.
entries.11:3: They accused Peter of visiting uncircumcised men and eating with them. Sharing a meal with outsiders was seen as breaking their rules.
entries.11:4: Peter patiently explained everything that had happened, step by step. When accused, it helps to calmly tell the whole story.
entries.11:5: Peter described praying in Joppa and seeing a vision of a large sheet coming down from heaven. God sometimes speaks to us in unexpected ways when we are seeking him.
entries.11:6: Looking closely, he saw all kinds of animals and birds in the sheet. The vision included creatures his law told him to avoid.
entries.11:7: A voice told him to get up and eat. God was directly asking him to do something he had always believed was wrong.
entries.11:8: Peter refused, saying he had never eaten anything unclean. His whole life had been shaped by these rules, so this was hard for him.
entries.11:9: The voice from heaven told him not to call common what God has made clean. God himself decides what is acceptable, not our traditions.
entries.11:10: This happened three times, then the sheet was taken back to heaven. The repetition showed Peter this was serious and from God.
entries.11:11: Right then, three men arrived at the house, sent from Caesarea. God's timing lined up exactly with the vision he had given.
entries.11:12: The Spirit told Peter to go with them without hesitation, and six brothers went along. God confirmed his direction with witnesses and clear guidance.
entries.11:13: The man told Peter how an angel had appeared and told him to send for Peter. God had been working on both sides of this meeting.
entries.11:14: Peter would share a message that could bring salvation to the man and his whole household. God's plan included this outsider and his family.
entries.11:15: While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit came on them just as it had on the Jewish believers at first. God gave clear proof he accepted them.
entries.11:16: Peter remembered Jesus' words that John baptized with water but they would be baptized with the Holy Spirit. Jesus' promise was coming true for these outsiders too.
entries.11:17: Since God gave them the same gift he gave us when they believed, Peter could not stand in God's way. We should not resist what God is clearly doing.
entries.11:18: Hearing this, the critics stopped arguing and praised God, saying he had given even non-Jews a changed heart and life. Honest evidence can turn opposition into worship.
entries.11:19: Believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen's death traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, sharing the message only with Jews at first. Trouble spread the message further than expected.
entries.11:20: Some of them, from Cyprus and Cyrene, began telling Greeks in Antioch the good news about Jesus. Some people step out and share with those others overlook.
entries.11:21: The Lord's power was with them, and many believed and turned to him. When God is at work, people's lives visibly change.
entries.11:22: News reached the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. Wise leaders check on what God is doing and send trusted people.
entries.11:23: Barnabas saw God's grace at work and was glad, and he urged them to stay close to the Lord with all their hearts. Good leaders encourage others to keep going.
entries.11:24: Barnabas was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and many more people came to the Lord. A faithful, Spirit-filled person can draw many to God.
entries.11:25: Barnabas then went to Tarsus to look for Saul. He recognized he needed help and went out of his way to find the right person.
entries.11:26: He found Saul and brought him to Antioch, where they taught the church for a year, and the disciples were first called Christians there. Steady teaching builds believers and gives them a clear identity.
entries.11:27: During that time, prophets came from Jerusalem to Antioch. God gives some people special insight to guide and warn his people.
entries.11:28: One prophet, Agabus, warned through the Spirit that a severe famine would spread across the whole world, which happened under Claudius. God can reveal what is coming so his people can prepare.
entries.11:29: The disciples decided, each according to what they could afford, to send help to the believers in Judea. When we hear of need, we should give as we are able.
entries.11:30: They did this, sending the gift to the church leaders by Barnabas and Saul. Generous help was handled through trusted leaders.
entries.12:1: King Herod began using his power to harm and arrest members of the church. It reminds readers that following Jesus can bring real opposition from powerful people.
entries.12:2: Herod had James, one of Jesus' closest followers, killed with a sword. It shows that faith can cost someone everything, even their life.
entries.12:3: Herod saw that killing James pleased the crowd, so he arrested Peter too during the Passover festival. It warns that leaders may do wrong things just to win public approval.
entries.12:4: Herod jailed Peter under heavy guard, planning to bring him out for trial after Passover. It shows how seriously Herod wanted to keep Peter from escaping.
entries.12:5: While Peter sat in prison, the church kept praying earnestly for him. It encourages readers to pray persistently for others who are in trouble.
entries.12:6: The night before his trial, Peter was asleep in chains between two guards with more watching the door. It shows how tightly he was guarded and how calm he was despite danger.
entries.12:7: A bright light appeared and an angel woke Peter, and the chains fell off his wrists. It shows God can break through any barrier to rescue someone.
entries.12:8: The angel told Peter to put on his shoes and coat and follow him. It shows that God's rescue still required Peter to get up and act.
entries.12:9: Peter followed the angel but thought he was only dreaming or seeing a vision. It reminds readers that God's help can seem too good to be true at first.
entries.12:10: They passed the guards and the iron gate opened by itself, then the angel left once Peter was on the street. It shows God guiding someone step by step until they are safe.
