entries.24:1: The high priest and some leaders came with a hired lawyer named Tertullus to bring formal charges against Paul before the governor Felix. It shows that powerful people were working together to accuse Paul and try to get him punished.
entries.24:2: Tertullus began his case by flattering Felix, claiming the governor had brought peace and good order to the nation. He was buttering him up before getting to the accusations, a common tactic in court.
entries.24:3: He kept piling on the praise, saying the people were deeply grateful to Felix everywhere. This was exaggerated flattery meant to win the governor's favor.
entries.24:4: He asked Felix to listen briefly and patiently, pretending to be considerate of the governor's time. It was a polite way of moving on to his accusations.
entries.24:5: He accused Paul of stirring up trouble among Jews everywhere and of being a ringleader of the group called the Nazarenes. This was a serious charge of causing unrest across the empire.
entries.24:6: He claimed Paul had even tried to make the Temple unclean, which is why they had seized him. This was a religious charge meant to make Paul look dangerous and disrespectful.
entries.24:7: This verse is missing from the earliest copies of Acts, so there is nothing reliable to explain.
entries.24:8: Tertullus said Felix could question Paul himself and find out that all their charges were true. He was inviting the governor to investigate, confident his case would hold up.
entries.24:9: The other Jewish leaders joined in, agreeing that these accusations were true. They backed up the lawyer's charges as a united front against Paul.
entries.24:10: Felix signaled Paul to speak, and Paul began politely, noting that Felix had judged the nation for many years. He was respectful but ready to defend himself.
entries.24:11: Paul pointed out that it had been only twelve days since he arrived in Jerusalem to worship. This short timeline made it easy to check the facts of what he had actually done.
entries.24:12: Paul said no one had seen him arguing with anyone or stirring up crowds in the Temple, synagogues, or city. He denied the charge of causing disturbances.
entries.24:13: He stated that his accusers could not prove any of the things they were now saying against him. Their charges were claims without evidence.
entries.24:14: Paul openly admitted he followed the Way, which his accusers called a false religion, but he insisted he still believed everything in the Law and the Prophets. He was loyal to the God of his ancestors and to the Scriptures.
entries.24:15: He shared the same hope his accusers had: that God will raise both good and bad people from the dead. This hope was central to his faith and his defense.
entries.24:16: Because of this hope, Paul said he always tried to keep a clear conscience before God and people. He aimed to live honestly and without shame.
entries.24:17: After several years away, Paul had come to Jerusalem to bring help and offerings to his own people. His visit was about charity, not trouble.
entries.24:18: He explained that he was in the Temple after being purified, quietly and with no crowd, when some Jews from Asia showed up. He was not leading a mob or causing a scene.
entries.24:19: Paul said those Jews from Asia should have come to court themselves if they had a complaint against him. The real accusers were absent.
entries.24:20: He challenged the men present to say what wrong they had seen him do when he stood before the council. He invited them to name any actual offense.
entries.24:21: The only thing he had shouted before the council was about being judged for his hope in the resurrection of the dead. That single statement was the real issue behind the case.
entries.24:22: Felix, who knew something about the Way, postponed the case until the commander Lysias could come down. He put off making a decision rather than settling it.
entries.24:23: Felix ordered that Paul be kept under guard but given freedom and allowed visits from his friends. Paul was treated fairly, not harshly, while awaiting trial.
entries.24:24: Some days later Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and sent for Paul to hear him talk about faith in Christ Jesus. The governor was curious about the Christian message.
entries.24:25: When Paul spoke about right living, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became afraid and sent him away for now. The message made him uncomfortable, so he put off dealing with it.
entries.24:26: Felix kept sending for Paul because he hoped Paul would pay him money for his release. His interest was greedy, not honest.
entries.24:27: After two years Festus replaced Felix, and Felix left Paul in chains to win favor with the Jews. Paul stayed imprisoned because of politics, not because he was guilty.
entries.25:1: Festus took over as governor and started his duties by traveling from Caesarea to Jerusalem. This shows he was getting to work right away in the area he now governed.
entries.25:2: The top religious leaders and important Jewish men brought formal accusations against Paul to the new governor. They were trying to get the case moving against him.
entries.25:3: They asked Festus to bring Paul to Jerusalem, but they were secretly planning to ambush and kill him on the road. Their request looked official but was really a murder plot.
entries.25:4: Festus refused, saying Paul was being held in Caesarea and that he would be going back there soon himself. He didn't fall for their plan.
entries.25:5: Festus invited the leaders to come with him and present any real charges against Paul. He was offering a fair hearing rather than just handing Paul over.
entries.25:6: After a short stay in Jerusalem, Festus returned to Caesarea and the next day held court and ordered Paul brought in. The case was moving forward officially.
entries.25:7: The Jewish leaders from Jerusalem surrounded Paul and made many serious accusations, but they couldn't prove any of them. Their charges were empty and unsupported.
entries.25:8: Paul defended himself, saying he had broken no Jewish law, done nothing wrong against the Temple, and committed no crime against Rome. He denied every charge against him.
entries.25:9: Festus, wanting to please the Jewish leaders, asked Paul if he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there. He was putting politics ahead of justice.
entries.25:10: Paul insisted he was standing before the proper Roman court and that he had done nothing wrong to the Jews, as Festus himself could see. He was asking for a fair trial where he legally stood.
entries.25:11: Paul said that if he deserved death he would accept it, but if the charges were false no one could hand him over to his enemies, so he appealed to Caesar. He was using his legal right as a Roman citizen.
entries.25:12: After discussing it with his advisors, Festus agreed to Paul's appeal and said he would send him to Caesar. The case was now headed to the emperor in Rome.
entries.25:13: Some days later, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived in Caesarea to pay a courtesy visit to Festus. This sets up the next scene in Paul's story.
entries.25:14: During their stay, Festus told Agrippa about Paul's case, explaining that Felix had left him in prison. He was briefing the king on the situation.
entries.25:15: Festus explained that the Jewish leaders had formally accused Paul and asked him to condemn the man. They wanted a quick guilty verdict.
entries.25:16: Festus told them it wasn't the Roman way to hand a man over without letting him face his accusers and answer the charges. He was insisting on a fair process.
entries.25:17: Festus said that when the accusers arrived, he didn't delay but held court the very next day and had Paul brought in. He moved the case along promptly.
entries.25:18: When the accusers spoke, they didn't bring the kind of serious crimes Festus expected. The charges turned out to be nothing like what he had assumed.
entries.25:19: Instead, the dispute was about their own religion and about a man named Jesus who had died but whom Paul claimed was alive. Festus saw it as an internal religious argument.
entries.25:20: Festus admitted he didn't know how to handle these religious questions, so he suggested Paul go to Jerusalem for trial. He was unsure how to judge the matter.
entries.25:21: But Paul appealed to have his case heard by Caesar, so Festus ordered him kept in custody until he could send him to the emperor. The appeal settled the next step.
entries.25:22: Agrippa told Festus he wanted to hear Paul himself, and Festus agreed to arrange it the next day. The king was curious about the case.
entries.25:23: The next day Agrippa and Bernice entered the hearing hall with great pomp, along with military commanders and city leaders, and Paul was brought in. It was a grand public occasion.
entries.25:24: Festus presented Paul to the crowd, saying the whole Jewish community had demanded his death both in Jerusalem and here. He was explaining why the case mattered.
entries.25:25: Festus stated his own view that Paul had done nothing deserving death, and since Paul had appealed to Caesar, he decided to send him. He was being honest about the lack of a capital charge.
entries.25:26: Festus said he had nothing definite to write to Caesar about Paul, so he brought him before Agrippa to get a clearer account after the hearing. He needed proper documentation for the emperor.
entries.25:27: Festus felt it made no sense to send a prisoner to Rome without stating the charges against him. He wanted the case properly explained before sending Paul on.
entries.26:1: The governor gives Paul permission to speak for himself, and Paul begins his defense with a simple gesture. It shows Paul getting a fair chance to explain his side.
entries.26:2: Paul tells the king he is glad to defend himself before someone who will actually listen. It's a polite opening that sets up his whole speech.
entries.26:3: Paul notes that Agrippa knows Jewish customs well, so he asks him to hear the case all the way through. He is appealing to the king's knowledge and fairness.
entries.26:4: Paul says everyone has known his way of life since he was young, both in his own region and in Jerusalem. His past is not a secret to anyone.
entries.26:5: His accusers could confirm that he lived as a strict Pharisee, the most serious group about keeping the law. He is showing he was once deeply devoted to his religion.
entries.26:6: Paul says he is on trial because he believes the promise God made to their ancestors. His hope in that promise is the real issue, not any crime.
entries.26:7: All twelve tribes of Israel have been earnestly serving God day and night, waiting for that same promise. Paul says he is being attacked for holding the very hope his people share.
entries.26:8: Paul asks why anyone would think it impossible for God to raise the dead. If God is God, bringing people back to life is not too hard for him.
entries.26:9: Paul admits he once thought it was his duty to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth. He is being honest about his own past mistakes.
entries.26:10: He carried this out in Jerusalem, putting many believers in prison with authority from the chief priests and voting against them when they were sentenced to death. He is not hiding how far he went.
entries.26:11: He punished believers in synagogues again and again, trying to force them to speak against God, and chased them even into distant towns. His opposition was fierce and relentless.
entries.26:12: Paul describes how he was traveling to Damascus with official authority and orders from the chief priests. He was on a mission to arrest believers.
entries.26:13: At midday on the road, a light brighter than the sun shone around him and his companions. It was a sudden, overwhelming heavenly sign.
entries.26:14: They all fell to the ground, and a voice spoke to him in Hebrew, asking why he was persecuting him and saying it was hard to fight against what was pushing him. God was confronting him directly.
entries.26:15: Paul asked who was speaking, and the answer was that it was Jesus himself, the one Paul was persecuting. Jesus identified himself with the believers Paul was hurting.
entries.26:16: Jesus told him to stand up because he had a purpose for him: to be a servant and a witness of what he had seen and would still see. Paul's life was being redirected toward a mission.
entries.26:17: Jesus promised to keep Paul safe from his own people and from the Gentiles, the non-Jewish nations he was being sent to. The mission would be dangerous, but God would protect him.
entries.26:18: Paul's job was to open people's eyes, turn them from darkness to light and from Satan's power to God, so they could receive forgiveness and a place among God's holy people through faith. This is the heart of the good news he preached.
entries.26:19: Paul says he did not disobey the heavenly vision he received. He responded to what God showed him.
entries.26:20: He preached in Damascus, Jerusalem, all Judea, and then to the Gentiles that people should turn from their sins to God and show that change by how they live. Real repentance produces real change in behavior.
entries.26:21: Because of this preaching, Jews seized him in the temple and tried to kill him. His message, not any crime, was the reason for the attack.
entries.26:22: With God's help Paul stands here today, telling both ordinary people and rulers what the prophets and Moses said would happen. His message is not new but was foretold long ago.
entries.26:23: The prophets said the Messiah would suffer, rise first from the dead, and bring light to both Jews and Gentiles. Paul says Jesus fulfilled exactly that.
entries.26:24: Festus interrupts loudly, saying Paul is out of his mind and that his great learning has driven him crazy. To Festus, the idea of a resurrection sounded like madness.
entries.26:25: Paul calmly denies it, telling Festus that what he says is true and sensible. He refuses to be rattled by the insult.
entries.26:26: Paul says the king knows about these events, so he speaks openly, because none of it happened in secret. The facts were public and could be checked.
entries.26:27: Paul turns to Agrippa and asks if he believes the prophets, adding that he is sure he does. He is steering the conversation toward a personal decision.
entries.26:28: Agrippa responds that Paul is close to persuading him to become a Christian. He is moved but not yet ready to commit.
entries.26:29: Paul says he prays to God that Agrippa and everyone listening would become like him, except for his chains. He wants them to share his faith, not his suffering.
entries.26:30: The king, the governor, Bernice, and the others stood up and left the room. The hearing was over.
entries.26:31: Outside, they agreed among themselves that Paul had done nothing deserving death or imprisonment. Even his judges saw he was innocent.
entries.26:32: Agrippa told Festus that Paul could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar. His legal appeal kept him in custody despite his innocence.
entries.27:1: Paul was being taken to Italy by ship as a prisoner, guarded by a Roman officer named Julius. It reminds us that even when we are not in control of our circumstances, God is still directing our path.
entries.27:2: They set sail on a ship headed for ports in Asia, and Paul's friend Aristarchus went with him. It shows that Paul was not alone in his hardship; friends stayed by his side.
entries.27:3: The next day they stopped at Sidon, and Julius treated Paul kindly, letting him visit his friends and rest. Small acts of kindness from people in authority can make a big difference to someone in trouble.
entries.27:4: They sailed again but had to keep close to the shelter of Cyprus because the wind was blowing against them. Sometimes progress is slow and difficult, and we have to adjust our plans.
entries.27:5: They sailed past the coasts of Cilicia and Pamphylia and arrived at Myra in Lycia. The journey continued step by step, just as life often moves forward one stage at a time.
entries.27:6: At Myra the officer found a ship from Alexandria heading for Italy and put them on board. Unexpected changes of plan can still be part of how God moves things along.
entries.27:7: Progress was slow for many days, and they struggled to get past Cnidus because of the wind, so they sailed along the sheltered side of Crete. Hard conditions can slow us down, but they don't stop God's purposes.
entries.27:8: They managed to reach a place called Fair Havens near the town of Lasea. Even in a difficult voyage, they found a place to stop and regroup.
entries.27:9: Much time had passed and sailing was now dangerous because it was late in the season, so Paul raised the matter with them. It's wise to speak up when we see danger ahead, even if others may not want to hear it.
entries.27:10: Paul warned them that the voyage would bring great loss, not only to the cargo and ship but to their lives. Honest warnings, even when unwelcome, can come from genuine concern for others.
entries.27:11: The officer trusted the ship's captain and owner more than he trusted Paul. People often rely on expert opinion over godly advice, and that can lead to trouble.
entries.27:12: The harbour wasn't suitable for wintering, so most of them decided to try to reach Phoenix, a better harbour in Crete. When people are eager to move on, they can ignore good advice and take risks.
entries.27:13: When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought their plan would work, so they set sail close to the shore of Crete. Good conditions at the start can make us overconfident about what lies ahead.
entries.27:14: Soon a violent wind called Euraquilo swept down on them. Storms can come suddenly, even when everything seemed fine just before.
entries.27:15: The ship was caught by the storm and couldn't sail into the wind, so they gave up steering and let it be driven along. Sometimes we have to stop fighting and trust God to carry us through.
entries.27:16: They passed the sheltered side of a small island called Cauda and, with great effort, managed to secure the ship's small boat. Even small rescues in a storm take hard work and deserve gratitude.
entries.27:17: They hauled the boat aboard and tied ropes around the ship to strengthen it, then lowered the sails for fear of being driven onto the sandbanks of Syrtis. When danger is real, it's wise to take practical steps to protect yourself and others.
entries.27:18: The storm kept battering them, so the next day they began throwing the cargo overboard. Sometimes we have to let go of valuable things to survive what we're facing.
entries.27:19: On the third day they threw the ship's sailing equipment overboard too. When things get desperate, even essential gear may have to be sacrificed to stay afloat.
entries.27:20: For many days they saw neither sun nor stars, and the storm pressed on them until all hope of being saved was gone. There are times when everything looks hopeless, and that is exactly when God can step in.
entries.27:21: After they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up and reminded them that they should have listened to his warning. It's painful to say "I told you so," but Paul used it to lead them toward hope.
entries.27:22: Paul told them to take heart because no one would lose their life, only the ship. God's promise of safety can lift people's spirits even in the worst circumstances.
entries.27:23: Paul said an angel of the God he serves came to him that night. God still speaks to those who belong to him, often in their darkest hours.
entries.27:24: The angel told Paul not to be afraid, because he would stand before Caesar, and God had given him everyone sailing with him. One person's faith can bring protection and hope to many others.
entries.27:25: Paul urged them to be encouraged because he trusted God to do exactly what he had been told. Faith in God's word is what keeps us steady when circumstances say otherwise.
entries.27:26: Paul added that they would run aground on a certain island. God's promises often include specific details that later prove true, building our confidence in him.
entries.27:27: On the fourteenth night, as they were being tossed around in the Adriatic Sea, the sailors sensed they were getting close to land. Even in confusion and darkness, people can sense when something is about to change.
entries.27:28: They measured the depth of the water and found it was about a hundred and twenty feet, then ninety feet a little later. Careful observation confirmed the danger was real and getting closer.
entries.27:29: Fearing they might hit rocks, they dropped four anchors from the back of the ship and prayed for daylight. When we can't see the way forward, prayer and holding steady are the right response.
entries.27:30: The sailors secretly tried to escape in the ship's boat, pretending they were going to lower anchors from the front. Fear can make people act selfishly, looking out only for themselves.
entries.27:31: Paul warned the officer and soldiers that unless the sailors stayed on board, no one would be saved. God's promises don't cancel our responsibility to act wisely and stay where we're told.
entries.27:32: The soldiers cut the ropes and let the boat drift away. Sometimes the only way to keep everyone safe is to remove the means of running away.
entries.27:33: As dawn approached, Paul urged everyone to eat, pointing out they had gone fourteen days without food. Practical care for the body matters, especially when people are exhausted and afraid.
entries.27:34: Paul asked them to eat for their own survival and assured them not a hair of their heads would be lost. Encouragement combined with practical action helps people keep going.
entries.27:35: Paul took bread, gave thanks to God in front of everyone, and then ate. Giving thanks in the middle of a crisis is a powerful witness to those watching.
entries.27:36: Everyone took heart and ate too. One person's calm faith and gratitude can lift the spirits of a whole group.
entries.27:37: There were two hundred and seventy-six people on board. It's worth remembering that God's promise covered every single person on that ship, not just Paul.
entries.27:38: After they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship by throwing the grain into the sea. Once people are strengthened, they can take the hard steps needed to survive.
entries.27:39: When daylight came, they didn't recognise the land but saw a sandy bay and decided to try to run the ship onto it. Even without full knowledge, they made a plan based on what they could see.
entries.27:40: They cut the anchors loose, untied the steering oars, raised the sail to the wind, and headed for the bay. After waiting and praying, they finally took action toward the shore.
entries.27:41: The ship ran aground on a sandbar, and while the front stayed stuck, the pounding waves broke the back apart. It means the ship was wrecked, and the people on board were now in real danger.
entries.27:42: The soldiers wanted to kill the prisoners so none could escape by swimming away. It shows how close Paul came to dying, not from the storm but from the guards.
entries.27:43: The officer in charge wanted to spare Paul, so he stopped the soldiers and ordered everyone who could swim to jump in and head for shore. It shows God quietly protecting Paul through a man who respected him.
entries.27:44: The others grabbed planks and pieces of the ship and made it to land too, so every single person survived. It means God kept his promise that no one on the ship would be lost.
entries.28:1: After the shipwreck everyone reached shore safely, and they learned the island was called Malta. It reminds the reader that God kept His promise to bring them through danger.
entries.28:2: The islanders were unusually kind, building a fire and sheltering the travelers from the rain and cold. Ordinary people can show real kindness to strangers in need.
entries.28:3: Paul gathered sticks for the fire, and a snake driven out by the heat bit his hand. Doing something helpful can still lead to unexpected trouble.
entries.28:4: The islanders assumed the snakebite proved Paul was a murderer whom justice had finally caught. People often jump to conclusions about why someone suffers.
entries.28:5: Paul simply shook the snake off into the fire and was not harmed. The danger was real, but it did not have the final say over him.
entries.28:6: The people expected Paul to swell up or drop dead, but when nothing happened they changed their minds and called him a god. Crowds can swing from one extreme judgment to another without knowing the truth.
entries.28:7: Nearby was land belonging to Publius, the island's leading official, who generously hosted the group for three days. God provided hospitality through an unexpected source.
entries.28:8: Publius's father was sick with fever and dysentery, and Paul prayed and laid hands on him and healed him. God's care reached into a stranger's household through Paul.
entries.28:9: After that healing, other sick people on the island came and were cured too. One act of mercy opened the door for many more.
entries.28:10: The islanders honored the group and supplied whatever they needed for the voyage when they left. Kindness given was returned in practical ways.
entries.28:11: After three months on the island, they set sail on an Alexandrian ship that had wintered there. Life moved forward again after a long, forced pause.
entries.28:12: They stopped at Syracuse and stayed there three days. Even the journey toward Rome had ordinary delays and stops.
entries.28:13: They sailed on to Rhegium, and a favorable south wind brought them to Puteoli the next day. Small shifts in circumstances can move things along quickly.
entries.28:14: In Puteoli they found some fellow believers and stayed with them a week before continuing to Rome. Finding family in faith along the way is a gift.
entries.28:15: Believers from Rome traveled out to meet Paul, and seeing them gave him courage and thanks to God. Support from others can strengthen a person facing a hard road.
entries.28:16: In Rome Paul was allowed to live in his own rented place, guarded by a soldier. Even in custody he was given room to keep serving.
entries.28:17: After three days Paul called the local Jewish leaders and explained that he had been arrested and handed to the Romans despite doing nothing against his people or their customs. He wanted them to hear his side directly.
entries.28:18: The Romans questioned him and found no reason to execute him, so they wanted to release him. His innocence was clear even to his captors.
entries.28:19: When his accusers objected, Paul had to appeal to Caesar, though he had nothing against his own nation. He was forced to take this step to protect himself, not out of hostility.
entries.28:20: Paul asked to meet them because the hope of Israel—the promised Messiah—was the very reason he was in chains. What looked like a criminal case was really about Israel's long-awaited hope.
entries.28:21: The leaders said they had received no letters or reports from Judea accusing Paul of anything. Not everyone had heard the charges against him.
entries.28:22: They wanted to hear Paul's own views, noting that this sect was spoken against everywhere. They were curious but already aware the movement was controversial.
entries.28:23: On the appointed day many came to Paul's lodging, and from morning to evening he explained the kingdom of God and argued from Moses and the prophets that Jesus is the promised one. He gave them a full, patient case from their own Scriptures.
entries.28:24: Some were persuaded by what Paul said, while others refused to believe. The same message can land very differently with different people.
entries.28:25: The group left divided, after Paul gave them one parting word from the prophet Isaiah. When people disagree about Jesus, the disagreement often runs deep.
entries.28:26: Isaiah was told the people would hear but not understand and look but not perceive. Hearing words is not the same as grasping their meaning.
entries.28:27: Their hearts had grown dull, their ears slow, and their eyes shut, so they would not turn to God and be healed. People can become so resistant that they shut out the very help they need.
entries.28:28: Paul declared that God's salvation had been sent to the Gentiles, and they would listen. When one group refuses the message, God opens the door to others.
entries.28:29: This verse is not included in the earliest manuscripts, so it is left out here. Its absence does not affect the story's meaning.
entries.28:30: Paul lived for two years in his rented house and welcomed everyone who came to visit him. Even under guard, he kept an open door for people.
entries.28:31: He boldly preached the kingdom of God and taught about Jesus Christ, and no one stopped him. The book ends with the gospel still advancing, even in Rome and even in chains.
